# Believable is not predictive: what three society simulations actually measured, and why our own model still scores below its prior

**TL;DR.** We read three society-simulation results in full today — Park et al.'s Generative Agents (2023), EconSimulacra (Hashimoto et al., arXiv:2606.26883), and a 2026 mobility-realism validation of AgentSociety and CitySim — and compared what each one actually measured against our own benchmark record. The pattern is the same at every scale: simulated people are easiest to make *believable*, harder to make *coupled across domains*, and hardest to make *predictively accurate against real human data*. Our own record sits at the hard end of that pattern: ManagerBench has a 192-row baseline, zero verified real intervention cases, and our Be.FM candidate scores 0.5556 against a 0.6111 prior — below it, so the prior still serves. This note shows the evidence, the tables, and the one validation step we are adding before any simulation result is allowed to shape an intervention.

*Audience: researchers and builders working on behavior simulation, synthetic users, or behavior intervention. We assume you know what an LLM agent is; we do not assume you have read these papers.*

## The problem

Our company definition is: simulate everything, then intervene. That order is only honest if the simulation is measured against something real. On 2026-11-24 we caught ourselves publishing research notes in a self-made "gate" format — checklists about our own specifications, with no data visualisation and no comparison against what the field has actually measured. A checklist about ourselves is a build note, not research. So today we went back to primary sources: what did the strongest society simulations measure, what numbers did they report, and where exactly does our own work stand on the same axes?

## How we did it

1. We re-read Park et al. (2023), "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior" (UIST '23), including the ablation table and the two-day end-to-end run.
2. We read EconSimulacra (Hashimoto, Kaneko, Ueda, Takayanagi & Izumi, arXiv:2606.26883), an open-source digital-twin platform that couples a consumer economy, mobility, and a social network through one shared internal state — stress. Its code, PyPI package, documentation, and live demo are all public, so a reader can run the same system we describe.
3. We read "When Plausible Is Not Realistic" (SIGSPATIAL 2026), which validates AgentSociety and CitySim mobility against real data from the Greater Paris region and Shanghai — the strongest "check the simulation against reality" design we found today.
4. We placed our own latest benchmark record next to them, unchanged: ManagerBench baseline 192 rows; verified real intervention cases 0; Manager v1 a negative result (below the base model, prior serving); Be.FM canonical accuracy 0.5556 (10/18) against a prior of 0.6111.

Failure before success, as our writing standard requires: our first attempt at today's note was another self-referential gate article. We discarded that format. What follows is the comparison itself.

## Evidence 1: believability is measurable — and it is not prediction

Park et al. populated Smallville with 25 agents, each seeded with one paragraph, driven by gpt-3.5-turbo, with a three-part architecture: a memory stream, reflection, and planning. One hundred human evaluators ranked interview answers from five conditions. The results (paper, Section 6.5.1):

| Condition | TrueSkill believability |
| --- | --- |
| Full architecture (memory + reflection + planning) | 29.89 |
| No reflection | 26.88 |
| No reflection, no planning | 25.64 |
| Human crowdworkers role-playing the agent | 22.95 |
| No memory, reflection, or planning | 21.21 |

In the two-day run, knowledge of a Valentine's Day party spread from 1 agent (4%) to 13 (52%), knowledge of a mayoral candidacy from 1 to 8 (32%), network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74, and 5 of the 12 agents who heard about the party attended it. Only 1.3% of 453 answers about other agents were hallucinated. Simulating those 25 agents for two days cost, in the authors' words, thousands of dollars in token credits and multiple days of wall-clock time.

What this measures is *believability to human raters* and *internal diffusion*. It does not measure whether a simulated person's next action matches a real person's next action. That distinction is the whole subject of this note.

## Evidence 2: coupling domains through one shared state

EconSimulacra asks a different question: can one internal state carry effects across domains? Each agent accumulates experiences in a consumer economy, in mobility, and on a social network; those experiences are converted into a shared stress level, and decisions in every domain read that same state. The case study is a restaurant promotion in a 10 x 10 grid world, run as 10 independent simulations for each of four model backbones (GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). The measured relationship is between online attention (daily social-media posts containing the keyword "pizza") and offline popularity (daily sales at the simulated restaurant):

```
online posts ──► visits ──► congestion ──► stress ──► fewer visits
      ▲                                                    │
      └────────────── posting about the experience ◄───────┘
        full model: positive linear term, negative quadratic term
        stress coupling removed (ablation): both effects weaken
```

With the stress mechanism, the fit shows the expected positive linear and negative quadratic coefficients — attention helps, then saturation and congestion dampen it — and discussion volume tracks sentiment diversity. Remove the stress coupling and both patterns weaken. This is a *stylised-fact reproduction*: the simulation is scored against a known qualitative shape from real socioeconomic data (Gong et al., 2025), not against individual-level ground truth.

## Evidence 3: against real mobility data, plausibility breaks

The Paris/Shanghai validation is the uncomfortable one. It scores AgentSociety and CitySim on mobility laws, temporal rhythms, network motifs, semantic activity transitions, and behavioral profiles, using real data from two regions. Its finding, in the authors' words, is a substantial gap between narrative plausibility and empirical mobility realism: the simulators capture some high-level semantic activity distributions, but struggle with trip-length distributions, origin-destination flows, dwell times, and transition dynamics — and realistic diversity is unstable across default prompting configurations.

In other words: an agent's day can read perfectly and still be wrong in every measurable distribution.

## Results: the same ladder, at every scale

| System | What was scored | Headline result | What it does not show |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generative Agents (2023) | Human-rated believability; in-world diffusion | Full architecture 29.89 vs 21.21 ablated; party knowledge 4% → 52% | Prediction of real individuals |
| EconSimulacra (2026) | Stylised-fact fit; ablation of stress coupling | Nonlinear online→offline pattern reproduced; weakens without coupling | Individual-level ground truth |
| AgentSociety / CitySim validation (2026) | Distributions vs real Paris & Shanghai data | Semantic distributions partly matched; trip lengths, OD flows, dwell times not matched | — (this is the reality check) |
| Anicca Manager / Be.FM (our record, 2026-11-24) | ManagerBench prediction vs prior | Be.FM 0.5556 vs prior 0.6111 — below prior; real intervention cases 0 | Any verified effect on a real person |

The ladder is consistent: believability is achievable today, stylised-fact coupling is achievable today, and distributional accuracy against real human data is where every system we read — including ours — currently fails or remains unproven.

## Trade-offs and limitations

We accepted one trade-off explicitly: we did not run EconSimulacra's LLM-backed simulation ourselves today, because running it requires paid model API calls, and our standing rule is that growth and research run on free, already-paid credit only. We read the paper, the public code, package, and documentation instead, and we label our non-run as exactly that. The cost of that choice is real: we cannot report our own replication numbers for its case study, only the authors' reported design and results.

A second limitation applies to the whole comparison: the four systems score different things, so the table compares *what kind of evidence each holds*, not a single shared metric. Anyone who collapses those rows into one ranking is making the fluency error this note is about.

## What we have not verified

- We have not replicated EconSimulacra's quadratic fit on any backbone. Unverified.
- We have not scored our own synthetic users against real distributional data the way the Paris/Shanghai study scores mobility. That is the gap, stated plainly.
- Our verified real intervention cases remain 0. No simulation result in this note changes that, and no intervention of ours is yet justified by a simulation that passed a reality check.

## What changes in our work

One concrete step, taken from the validation paper's design: before a Manager simulation may shape an intervention, it must pass a distributional check against real data we already hold — the same move as scoring trip lengths against Paris data, applied to our own domain (for example, the distribution of times at which real users open the app, against the distribution our synthetic users produce). Believability reviews stay, but they no longer count as validation. Our next research note will report the first such check, with its distributions shown, whatever the result.

## Try it

- Run the system we describe: EconSimulacra is open source — code at https://github.com/SimulacraBusiness/econsimulacra , package on PyPI, documentation and a live demo linked from the paper page below.
- Read our open numbers, updated daily: https://aniccaai.com/open/
- Our intervention product, whose effects remain unproven until the checks above pass: [Anicca](/affirmation-app). More notes in our [Research hub](/blog/c/research).

## Further reading

- Park et al. (2023), Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior — https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3586183.3606763?cookieSet=1
- Hashimoto et al., EconSimulacra: A Digital Twin Platform of Socio-Economic Systems Powered by LLM Agents — https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26883
- When Plausible Is Not Realistic: Evaluating Human Mobility in LLM-Based Urban Simulation — https://arxiv.org/html/2606.13835
- AgentSociety Challenge (Web Conference 2025): 295 teams, over 1,400 submissions, winning user-modeling designs improved 21.9% in the development phase — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3701716.3719233

Sources and dates: all external numbers above are from the papers as read on 2026-11-24 and are attributed in place. Our own numbers are from our internal benchmark record as of 2026-11-24 (ManagerBench baseline 192 rows; Be.FM 0.5556 = 10/18 against prior 0.6111; verified real intervention cases 0).
